old_html_inputs: Affordability Ceiling; Membership or Nothing; Ritual Economy
first_principles_point: Value retail is the business of lowering purchase regret for households under pressure.
money_path: household budget pressure -> retail format choice -> sales/fees/ads -> inventory turn -> margin -> cash
company_examples: Costco; Walmart; Target; Dollar General; Burlington; TJX; Ollies
proof_needed: traffic; ticket; basket; membership; inventory; shrink; OCF; FCF
safe_use: Safe claim: value retail is regret reduction, not simply cheapness.

first_principles_point: A pressured household still spends, but it sorts spending by which trip feels safest, smartest, and least wasteful.
money_path: fixed bills -> constrained flexible budget -> format choice -> basket -> margin/cash test
company_examples: Costco; Walmart; Dollar General; Target; Burlington
proof_needed: household spend mix; traffic; basket; trip frequency; margin; cash flow
safe_use: Safe claim: household pressure changes spending routes, not all demand.

first_principles_point: The affordability ceiling is the point where mistakes become too expensive for ordinary households.
money_path: fixed household costs -> smaller flexible budget -> value traffic or trade-down -> margin and cash test
company_examples: Walmart; Costco; Dollar General; Dollar Tree; Burlington; TJX; Ross; Target
proof_needed: price/mix; comps; unit volume; margins; inventory; consumer commentary
safe_use: Safe claim: affordability pressure changes where spending feels safe.

first_principles_point: Price regret is the fear of overpaying; the retailer must lower that fear without destroying margin.
money_path: price anxiety -> trusted low-price format -> traffic/basket -> gross margin -> cash conversion
company_examples: Costco; Walmart; Dollar General; Dollar Tree; Aldi; Kroger; BJ's
proof_needed: price gaps; traffic; basket; private label; gross margin; shrink; OCF
safe_use: Safe claim: low price matters only when it converts to repeat cash.

first_principles_point: Trip regret is the fear that shopping wastes time, fuel, attention, or effort.
money_path: task burden -> one-stop or high-value trip -> basket consolidation -> store/ecommerce/ads/membership economics
company_examples: Walmart; Target; Costco; Kroger; Amazon; Dollar General
proof_needed: traffic; basket; delivery/pickup cost; marketplace; ads; membership; OCF
safe_use: Safe claim: one-stop convenience must still pay after fulfillment cost.

first_principles_point: Access regret is the fear that basics are not reachable when time, transport, or cash are constrained.
money_path: nearby need -> small basket -> consumables visit -> gross margin after labor and shrink -> cash
company_examples: Dollar General; Dollar Tree; Walmart neighborhood formats; pharmacies; convenience stores
proof_needed: store density; traffic; ticket; consumables mix; labor; shrink; store standards
safe_use: Safe claim: proximity is value, but access traffic can still be low-margin.

first_principles_point: Status regret is the fear that budget pressure erases identity; off-price formats preserve branded access.
money_path: identity/gift need -> off-price discovery -> traffic -> merchandise margin -> inventory turn -> cash
company_examples: Burlington; TJX; Ross; Ollies; Macys; Nike wholesale
proof_needed: traffic; merchandise margin; branded supply; markdowns; inventory turn; shrink
safe_use: Safe claim: off-price growth depends on merchandise access and execution.

first_principles_point: Membership can turn value retail from a transaction into a recurring relationship and trust shortcut.
money_path: membership/loyalty -> repeated trip/data relationship -> basket concentration -> supplier/ads/private-label/service monetization
company_examples: Costco; Walmart; Target; Amazon; BJs; Sams Club; Kroger
proof_needed: membership fees; renewal; traffic; basket; private label; ad revenue; retention
safe_use: Safe claim: membership shows relationship potential, not permanent loyalty.

first_principles_point: Routine spending survives pressure when a retailer makes basics and small pleasures feel responsible.
money_path: household routine -> repeat trip/order -> replenishment plus treat -> basket and margin -> cash
company_examples: Walmart; Costco; Target; Dollar General; Dollar Tree; Ollies; Kroger; Chewy
proof_needed: repeat purchase; basket mix; seasonal sales; private label; gross margin; cash
safe_use: Safe claim: routine helps demand, but still needs margin and cash proof.

first_principles_point: Private label turns retailer trust into both customer savings and potential margin protection.
money_path: price pressure -> store-brand trial -> repeat purchase -> margin benefit -> inventory/cash conversion
company_examples: Costco; Walmart; Target; Kroger; Aldi; Dollar General; Dollar Tree
proof_needed: private-label penetration; repeat; margin; price gap; inventory turn; customer trust
safe_use: Safe claim: private label works only if quality protects trust.

first_principles_point: Inventory reveals whether the value proposition is real or just a story waiting for markdowns.
money_path: merchandise buy -> sell-through -> markdown/shrink/freight/labor -> gross margin -> OCF
company_examples: Target; Burlington; TJX; Ross; Dollar General; Walmart; Costco; Ollies
proof_needed: inventory turns; aging; markdowns; shrink; freight; gross margin; OCF
safe_use: Safe claim: inventory quality is a core proof point.

first_principles_point: Retailers can monetize traffic through ads, credit, marketplace, seller services, and membership layers.
money_path: shopper traffic/data -> ad/seller/credit/service revenue -> profit contribution -> trust/regulatory risk check
company_examples: Walmart; Target; Amazon; Macys; Costco co-brands; Kroger
proof_needed: ad revenue; credit income; seller fees; membership; margin contribution; trust risk
safe_use: Safe claim: relationship monetization is not proof the core basket is healthy.

first_principles_point: Shrink and store execution decide whether traffic can become cash.
money_path: inventory purchase -> store control/availability -> shrink/markdown/loss -> gross margin -> cash
company_examples: Target; Dollar General; Dollar Tree; Walmart; Burlington; TJX; Ross
proof_needed: shrink; out-of-stock; labor; store standards; gross margin bridge; inventory loss
safe_use: Safe claim: traffic can grow while economics leak through shrink.

first_principles_point: The proof ladder runs from pressure visibility to trip-job visibility to customer signals to operating conversion to durable value proof.
money_path: pressure -> trip job -> customer signal -> operating conversion -> cohort/cash durability
proof_needed: comps; traffic; ticket; basket; membership; inventory; shrink; OCF; FCF; cohorts
safe_use: Safe claim: current evidence reaches levels 1-4 in pieces; level 5 remains open.

first_principles_point: Each value format needs different proof: club, mass, dollar, off-price, closeout, and mid-market formats do not prove the theme the same way.
money_path: format -> correct metric -> cash-quality bridge -> safe claim or gap
company_examples: Costco; Walmart; Target; Dollar General; Burlington; TJX; Ollies; Macys
proof_needed: format-specific metrics; margin; inventory; fulfillment; renewal; cash flow
safe_use: Safe claim: no one retail metric proves value durability.

first_principles_point: The next proof pass should go below comps into traffic/ticket, units, renewal, inventory, shrink, fulfillment, ads, OCF, and FCF.
money_path: source pull -> retailer-by-retailer cash-quality table -> durable value proof boundary
company_examples: Costco; Walmart; Target; Dollar General; Burlington
proof_needed: traffic/ticket; units/price; renewal; inventory; shrink; markdowns; OCF; FCF
safe_use: Safe claim: this page defines the next cash-quality extraction path; it is not extraction itself.
